before.answer: EU probes cloud egress fees to prevent vendor lock-in, focusing on pricing for partial workloads moving between services."

after.answer: EU probes if cloud egress fees are designed to prevent customers from switching providers.

The European Commission has launched a formal investigation into cloud egress fees charged by Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, examining whether these fees are designed to make it irrational for customers to switch providers. While current egress costs can be up to fifty times higher than storage costs, the regulators focus specifically on scenarios where customers retain one workload and migrate only another. The investigation centers on whether the fees are structured to lock customers into a single vendor rather than reflecting actual costs. Although all three providers have reduced egress pricing over the past 18 months and now waive fees for full exits, regulators are scrutinizing the practice of charging exorbitant fees for data movement. If found abusive, the Commission could mandate transparent, per-gigabyte pricing in a standardized format—similar to how it has required telecoms roaming pricing transparency. This move aims to promote fair competition and prevent anti-competitive behavior in cloud computing services.
The laptop lasted nine hours of real work, which is less than the fourteen hours claimed on the box.

To find the percentage shorter:

Difference = 14 - 9 = 5 hours  
Percentage shorter = (5 / 14) × 100 ≈ 35.7%

So, the real-world battery life is about **35.7% shorter** than the claim on the box.

Articles about cloud egress fees include:

- [1] EU regulators open formal probe into cloud egress fees: The European Commission launched a formal investigation into egress fees charged by AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, questioning whether the fees are designed to make switching irrational [1].

- [2] Cloud providers race to publish egress fee schedules: Following the probe, two of the three providers released revised pricing with per-region transfer costs, though analysts note the tables lack comparability across providers [2].

- [3] Egress fees and the shape of lock-in: Analyzes egress fees as a disclosure issue, arguing that while egress is the only visible line item in cloud lock-in, its regulation may not significantly reduce overall vendor lock-in without comparable pricing for other costs [3].
